items.bodyEn: Leaving Fujisawa, travelers crossed the Banyū River, the lower Sagami, by ferry to reach Hiratsuka, one of the smaller post towns. Hiroshige's print, Hiratsuka: Nawate Road, shows a courier running along a zigzag path between fields, the rounded hump of Kōrai-yama ahead and the white peak of Fuji behind it.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō series (c. 1833), print 'Hiratsuka: Nawate Road' (縄手道)

items.titleEn: Why 七夕 Reads たなばた
items.bodyEn: The characters 七夕 mean seventh evening, yet the word is read tanabata, a reading that ignores them. It comes from 棚機, a loom, and the loom maiden who wove cloth for the gods in old Japanese rites. When the Chinese star festival of the seventh night arrived, it merged with this native word.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (Shōgakukan), entry たなばた: 棚機・棚機つ女

items.bodyEn: On Tanabata, the seventh of July, people write wishes on narrow paper strips called tanzaku and tie them to bamboo branches. The festival retells the meeting of the weaver star Vega and the herder star Altair across the Milky Way, allowed once a year. Hiratsuka's own Tanabata festival, now among Japan's largest, began in 1951.

items.titleEn: とても Once Meant Not at All
items.bodyEn: Until the early 1900s とても appeared only with negatives: とても無理だ, utterly impossible. Using it as a plain intensifier, とても大きい, spread in Tokyo during the 1910s and 1920s and was remarked on by writers as a new fashion. Today both patterns are standard, while あまり, not very, still pairs mostly with a negative.
items.ja: とても{大|おお}きいです。
